title: Questions to Ask About Their Architecture and Team
summary: The design-specific version of "any questions for me?" — asking about their real scaling story, on-call load, and technical debt instead of generic culture questions.

slides.markdown:
"Any questions for me?" at the end of a design round is still an evaluated moment, and most candidates waste it on generic questions about culture or growth opportunities that could apply to any company. In a design-specific round, the stronger move is asking about their actual architecture, scaling story, and on-call reality.

This topic covers what to ask instead, and why it signals genuine technical curiosity rather than a rehearsed closing question.

slides.sectionTitle: Why this moment is still evaluated, and why generic questions waste it
slides.markdown:
It's tempting to treat "any questions for me?" as the interview winding down, but interviewers are still forming an impression during your questions — often about whether you're genuinely curious about the engineering, or just going through the motions of a checklist.

A generic question like "what's the culture like?" or "what growth opportunities are there?" could be asked of any company in any industry, which is exactly the problem — it signals you didn't engage with what you just spent the last 45 minutes discussing. In a system-design-specific round, the strongest questions come directly from what you just heard about their architecture.

The broader idea that this closing moment is a two-way signal — you're evaluating them as much as they're evaluating you — is covered generically for the behavioral round elsewhere in this interview-prep track. This topic builds specifically on that framing, applied to a system-design context: instead of generic culture or growth questions, you're using the moment to genuinely learn about the architecture, team, and operational reality you'd be joining.

If you've already internalized the general version of "good questions signal genuine engagement, not just politeness," the design-specific version here is the same principle aimed at a different set of topics: scale, ownership, debt, and decision process.

A few questions consistently land well because they show you're thinking about the system the way an owner would, not just a visitor. "What's the part of the system you'd redesign if you had the resources to do it?" invites the interviewer to be candid about weaknesses, which is genuinely useful information and shows you expect real systems to have imperfect parts. "How do architecture decisions actually get made here — one senior engineer, a design-review committee, consensus?" tells you how you'd actually operate day to day, and shows you understand that process shapes outcomes as much as any single decision.

Both questions work because they can only be asked by someone who was actually listening to the round, not by someone reciting a memorized list.

Using these four categories as a mental checklist means you're never stuck for a good question, even in a round where nothing specific stood out to riff on directly.

slides.sectionTitle: Questions that surface real signal: on-call, incidents, decision-making
slides.markdown:
Beyond sounding senior, some questions genuinely surface information you'd want before joining. "What's on-call like for this team — how often does someone get paged, and for what?" tells you about operational health more honestly than almost anything in a job posting. "What was the biggest incident this system has had, and what changed afterward?" tells you whether the team actually learns from failures or just patches them.

These aren't just performative — the answers materially affect what it's like to work there, so asking them serves your own decision-making as much as it signals engagement to the interviewer.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: a question that signals curiosity vs one that signals you didn't listen
slides.markdown:
| | Signals you didn't listen | Signals genuine curiosity |
|---|---|---|
| Example | "What's the tech stack?" (already covered in the round) | "You mentioned the write path goes through a queue — what happens when a consumer falls behind?" |
| Basis | Generic, could be asked before the interview started | Built directly on something said in the last 45 minutes |
| What it tells the interviewer | You were waiting for your turn to speak | You were engaged with the specifics the whole time |
| Cost if unanswerable | Wastes the closing moment | Even a partial answer gives you real signal back |

The fastest way to generate the right-column question is to jot down one thing during the round you wanted to know more about, and ask that.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: asking a question the job description already answered
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Any question is better than no question, so I'll ask something safe I prepared in advance."

**Why it's wrong:** if the answer was already stated in the job description or the interviewer said it earlier in the same conversation, asking it signals you weren't paying attention rather than that you're curious — the opposite of the intended effect, and worse than it would have been to ask nothing.

**Correct model:** prepare one or two category-level questions as a fallback (scale, ownership, debt, decision process), but prioritize a question built from something specific the interviewer actually said in this round — it's both more genuine and impossible to have prepared as a generic script.
